---
key: halpern2025causality
title: "Causality Without Causal Models"
authors: "Halpern & Pass"
year: 2025
venue: "TARK 2025; EPTCS 437, pp. 160-174"
url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.21260v1
checked: 2026-11-01
tags: [source:formal-sweep-2026-11-01, contribution:theory, motivation:explainability]
---
**TL;DR** Generalizes actual causation and causal explanation beyond structural causal models while recovering Halpern–Pearl definitions under suitable restrictions.
**Problem** Structural-model definitions restrict causal claims and exclude backtracking.
**Method** Abstract counterfactual semantics; parameterized witness languages; equivalence proofs for causation and explanation.
**Findings** Supports disjunctions, modalities and nested counterfactuals; recovers modified Halpern–Pearl definitions in specified settings; permits backtracking.
**Limits** Witness languages change causal judgments. Equivalence requires particular language, correspondence and compatibility conditions; structural-model results concern recursive models. No empirical evaluation.

**Relations**
- (none)

**New tags**
- source:formal-sweep-2026-11-01: added through the formal-definition literature sweep of 1 November 2026.

definitions.quote: Formally, a causal model M is a pair (S , F ), where S is a signature, which explicitly lists the endogenous and exogenous variables and characterizes their possible values, and F defines a set of (modifiable) structural equations, relating the values of the variables.
definitions.formula: M=(\mathcal S,\mathcal F),\quad \mathcal S=(\mathcal U,\mathcal V,\mathcal R),\quad F_X:\left(\prod_{U\in\mathcal U}\mathcal R(U)\right)\times\left(\prod_{Y\in\mathcal V\setminus\{X\}}\mathcal R(Y)\right)\to\mathcal R(X).
definitions.assumptions: Specified variables, nonempty ranges and deterministic structural equations. The paper restricts to recursive models and finite endogenous variables and ranges.
definitions.gloss: A system of equations determines endogenous variables from other variables and background conditions.
definitions.relation: Supplies the structural setting for Definition 2.1 and the intervention semantics generalized by causal-counterfactual families.

definitions.quote: Intuitively, [Y1 ← y1 , . . . ,Yk ← yk ]ϕ says that ϕ would hold if Yi were set to yi , for i = 1, . . . , k.
definitions.formula: (M,\vec u)\models[\vec Y\leftarrow\vec y]\varphi\iff(M_{\vec Y\leftarrow\vec y},\vec u)\models\varphi,\qquad F^{\vec Y\leftarrow\vec y}_{Y_i}=y_i.
definitions.assumptions: Recursive causal model, fixed context, distinct intervention variables and admissible values; other equations remain unchanged.
definitions.gloss: Evaluate a claim after replacing the selected variables’ equations with constant assignments.
definitions.relation: Special case of the paper’s extended counterfactual semantics when the antecedent is a conjunction of primitive events.

definitions.quote: Definition 2.1: ⃗X =⃗x is an actual cause of ϕ in the causal setting (M,⃗u) if the following three conditions hold:
definitions.formula: \begin{aligned}\mathrm{AC1}:&\ (M,\vec u)\models(\vec X=\vec x)\land\varphi.\\\mathrm{AC2}:&\ \exists\vec W\subseteq\mathcal V\setminus\vec X,\vec w^*,\vec x' :\ (M,\vec u)\models\vec W=\vec w^*\ \land\ (M,\vec u)\models[\vec X\leftarrow\vec x',\vec W\leftarrow\vec w^*]\neg\varphi.\\\mathrm{AC3}:&\ \nexists\vec X'\subsetneq\vec X\text{ whose actual assignment satisfies AC2}.\end{aligned}
definitions.assumptions: Known recursive causal model and actual context. Witness variables are fixed at actual values. The PDF’s AC2 quantifier prints an unprimed alternative; the intervention uses x′.
definitions.gloss: An actual, minimal event prevents the outcome when changed while some other variables retain their actual values.
definitions.relation: Recovered by abstract actual causation in Theorem 4.2; generalized to suitable recursive counterfactual structures in Theorem 4.5.

definitions.quote: A ccf M is a family of models or structures (we use the latter two words more or less interchangeably) such that each model M ∈ M has a set of possible states or worlds, and there is a semantics that allows us to define (M, w) |= ϕ for all formulas in a language L M . We require that L M include primitive events in some signature S , and be closed under conjunction and negation (so contains L (S )) and basic counterfactuals, so that if ϕ and ψ are in L (S ), then ϕ → ψ ∈ L M .
definitions.assumptions: Models with states, primitive-event interpretations and a truth semantics supporting the stated Boolean and counterfactual language.
definitions.gloss: A shared semantic framework in which causal definitions can use counterfactuals without requiring structural equations.
definitions.relation: Includes causal models and Lewis-style counterfactual structures; supports abstract actual causation and abstract explanation.

definitions.term: counterfactual in causal models with an arbitrary Boolean antecedent
definitions.quote: To give semantics to a counterfactual of the form ϕ → ψ ∈ L + (S ), we proceed as follows: Let ⃗Y be the endogenous variables that appear in ϕ. Then we take (M,⃗u) |= ϕ → ψ iff there exists a vector ⃗y of values such that ϕ ∧ ⃗Y = ⃗y is consistent (when viewed as a propositional formula) and (M,⃗u) |= [⃗Y ←⃗y]ψ.
definitions.formula: (M,\vec u)\models\varphi\to\psi\iff\exists\vec y\in\mathcal R(\vec Y):\ \operatorname{Consistent}(\varphi\land\vec Y=\vec y)\land(M,\vec u)\models[\vec Y\leftarrow\vec y]\psi,\quad\vec Y=\operatorname{Vars}(\varphi).
definitions.assumptions: Recursive causal model; intervene on exactly the endogenous variables occurring in the antecedent; consistency is propositional.
definitions.gloss: Some complete assignment satisfying the antecedent must make the consequent true when imposed.
definitions.relation: Extends basic causal formulas; differs from universal closest-world semantics for nonbinary negated antecedents.

definitions.quote: That is, (M, s) |= ϕ → ψ if in all the closest states to s satisfying ϕ, ψ also holds. (It follows that (M, s) |= ϕ → ψ vacuously if there are no states t such that (M,t) |= ϕ.)
definitions.formula: M=(S,R,\pi),\quad t\preceq_s u\iff(s,t,u)\in R;\qquad(M,s)\models\varphi\to\psi\iff\forall t\in\operatorname{Min}_{\preceq_s}\{v:(M,v)\models\varphi\},\ (M,t)\models\psi.
definitions.assumptions: Finite state set; reflexive, transitive closeness relations; each state is strictly closer to itself than any other state.
definitions.gloss: The consequent must hold in every closest world where the antecedent holds.
definitions.relation: An alternative counterfactual semantics supporting the same abstract causation and explanation definitions; can allow backtracking.

definitions.term: actual cause with respect to CX
definitions.quote: Definition 4.1: Given a ccf M and set CX ⊆ L M of formulas, ϕ is an actual cause of ψ with respect to CX in a model M ∈ M and state s if the following three conditions hold:
definitions.formula:
egin{aligned}\mathrm{AC1'}:&\ (M,s)\models\varphi\land\psi.\\mathrm{AC2'}:&\ \exists	au\in C_X:\ (M,s)\models	au\land((
eg\varphi\land	au)	o
eg\psi).\\mathrm{AC3'}:&\ 
exists\varphi'\in C_X:\ (\models\varphi\Rightarrow\varphi')\land(
ot\models\varphi'\Rightarrow\varphi)\land\mathrm{AC2'}(\varphi',\psi).\end{aligned}
definitions.assumptions: Chosen ccf, model, state, counterfactual semantics and admissible witness language C_X. Logical implication and counterfactual implication are distinct.
definitions.gloss: A true, logically minimal condition is causally necessary once an admissible true witness is retained.
definitions.relation: Generalizes modified HP actual causation; allows complex causes and depends on the witness language.

definitions.quote: As is standard, we say that an agent knows ϕ if ϕ is true at all the settings in K .
definitions.assumptions: Epistemic state K consisting of contexts of a fixed causal model; the agent’s uncertainty is represented by membership in K.
definitions.gloss: An agent knows a statement when it holds in every situation the agent considers possible.
definitions.relation: Makes explanation agent-relative and motivates the additional nontriviality condition.

definitions.quote: Definition 6.1: ⃗X = ⃗x is an explanation of ψ in a model M relative to a set K of contexts in M if the following conditions hold:
definitions.formula: \begin{aligned}\mathrm{EX1(a)}:&\ \forall\vec u\in K,\ (M,\vec u)\models\vec X=\vec x\land\psi\Rightarrow\exists(X=x)\in(\vec X=\vec x),\vec Y=\vec y:\ X=x\land\vec Y=\vec y\text{ is a cause of }\psi.\\\mathrm{EX1(b)}:&\ \forall\vec u'\in K,\ (M,\vec u')\models[\vec X\leftarrow\vec x]\psi.\\\mathrm{EX2}:&\ \nexists\vec X'\subsetneq\vec X\text{ satisfying EX1(a), EX1(b) with the restricted assignment}.\\\mathrm{EX3}:&\ \exists\vec u\in K:\ (M,\vec u)\models\vec X=\vec x\land\psi.\end{aligned}
definitions.assumptions: Known recursive causal model, epistemic context set K and modified HP actual causation. Causes may contain additional conjuncts outside the explanation.
definitions.gloss: An explanation is minimally sufficient throughout the agent’s possibilities and contains something causally relevant wherever it actually holds.
definitions.relation: The HP explanation definition reviewed by the paper; generalized by Definition 6.3.

definitions.term: nontrivial explanation in a causal model
definitions.quote: The explanation is nontrivial if it also satisfies EX4.
definitions.formula: \mathrm{EX1\text{--}EX3}\quad\land\quad\exists\vec u'\in K:\ (M,\vec u')\models\neg(\vec X=\vec x)\land\psi.
definitions.assumptions: An explanation satisfying Definition 6.1 and an epistemic state containing an outcome-compatible context where the explanation is false.
definitions.gloss: Observing the outcome does not already tell the agent that the explanation holds.
definitions.relation: Adds an epistemic informativeness requirement to explanation; mirrored by EX4′ in the abstract framework.

definitions.quote: Definition 6.3: Given a ccf M and set CX ⊆ L M of formulas, ϕ is an explanation of ψ with respect to CX in a model M ∈ M and state s relative to a set K of states in M if the following three conditions hold:
definitions.formula:
egin{aligned}\mathrm{EX1(a)'}:&\  orall s\in K,\ (M,s)\models\varphi\land\psi\Rightarrow\exists	au_1,	au_2\in C_X:\ 
ot\models	au_1,\ \models\varphi\Rightarrow	au_1,\ \models	au_2\Rightarrow	au_1,\ \operatorname{Cause}_{C_X}(	au_2,\psi;M,s).\\mathrm{EX1(b)'}:&\  orall s'\in K,\ (M,s')\models\varphi	o\psi.\\mathrm{EX2'}:&\ 
exists\varphi':\ (\models\varphi\Rightarrow\varphi')\land(
ot\models\varphi'\Rightarrow\varphi)\land\mathrm{EX1'}(\varphi',\psi).\\mathrm{EX3'}:&\ \exists s\in K:\ (M,s)\models\varphi\land\psi.\end{aligned}
definitions.assumptions: Ccf and counterfactual semantics, admissible formula set C_X, epistemic state set K and Definition 4.1 causation. Minimality ranges over formulas, not merely variable subsets.
definitions.gloss: A minimally sufficient formula must share a nontrivial logical consequence with an actual cause wherever explanation and outcome coexist.
definitions.relation: Generalizes Definition 6.1 under Theorem 6.4’s language restriction; Theorem 6.5 establishes correspondence for compatible recursive structures.

definitions.term: nontrivial explanation with respect to CX
definitions.quote: Again, the explanation is nontrivial if EX4′ .
definitions.formula: \mathrm{EX1'\text{--}EX3'}\quad\land\quad\exists s'\in K:\ (M,s')\models\neg\varphi\land\psi.
definitions.assumptions: An abstract explanation and an epistemic state permitting the outcome without the explanation.
definitions.gloss: The explanation supplies information not already settled by the outcome.
definitions.relation: Abstract counterpart of EX4 in Definition 6.1.

---
key: beckers2022causal
title: "Causal Explanations and XAI"
authors: "Beckers"
year: 2022
venue: "CLeaR 2022"
url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.13169v2
checked: 2026-11-01
tags: [source:formal-sweep-2026-11-01, contribution:theory, motivation:explainability]
---
**TL;DR** Defines action-guiding causal explanations and derives actual causation from sufficient explanations, exposing distinctions hidden by independent-input assumptions.
**Problem** Predictive explanations can misguide actions when features causally affect one another.
**Method** Deterministic structural models; sufficiency networks, witnesses, explanation dominance and replacement criteria.
**Findings** Connects sufficient and counterfactual explanations to actual causes; proves independence collapses distinct causal notions; proposes fairness based on actual causes.
**Limits** Assumes perfect causal knowledge, strong recursivity and restrictive agreement with the predictor. Probabilistic, approximate and practical computation extensions remain future work.

**Relations**
- (none)

**New tags**
- source:formal-sweep-2026-11-01: added through the formal-definition literature sweep of 1 November 2026.

definitions.quote: Definition 2 A causal model M is a pair (S, F ), where S is a signature and F defines a function that associates with each endogenous variable X a structural equation FX giving the value of X in terms of the values of other endogenous and exogenous variables.
definitions.formula: M=(\mathcal S,\mathcal F),\quad\mathcal S=(\mathcal U,\mathcal V,\mathcal R),\quad F_X:\mathcal R(\mathcal U\cup\mathcal V\setminus\{X\})\to\mathcal R(X).
definitions.assumptions: Deterministic structural equations and nonempty variable ranges. The paper restricts to strongly recursive models.
definitions.gloss: Structural equations specify how variables respond to their causes and to interventions.
definitions.relation: Foundational model for all subsequent sufficiency, explanation and actual-causation definitions.

definitions.quote: A first requirement is that such a causal model is consistent with the ML-model, meaning that they at least agree on how to classify all observations.
definitions.formula: \mathcal V=\vec I\cup\{Y\};\quad\forall V_i\in\mathcal V,\ \operatorname{Pa}(V_i)\cap\mathcal U\in\{\varnothing,\{U_i\}\};\quad\forall\vec i,y:\ \bigl(M\models(\vec I=\vec i\Rightarrow Y=y)\bigr)\iff h(\vec i)=y.
definitions.assumptions: A deterministic predictor h and causal model of its target domain. Each variable with an exogenous parent has a unique single such parent, as specified in Definition 3.
definitions.gloss: The causal model matches the predictor on observations and satisfies the paper’s restricted variable structure.
definitions.relation: Agreement is weaker than agreement under interventions; used with Independence in the collapse theorems.

definitions.quote: As knowledge of the causal model is hard to come by many approaches to actionguiding explanations ignore it entirely and assume that the input variables are causally independent (Sharma et al., 2020; Ustun et al., 2019; Poyiadzi et al., 2020; Kommiya Mothilal et al., 2021).
definitions.formula: \forall I_a,I_b\in\vec I:\ I_a\notin\operatorname{Pa}(I_b).
definitions.assumptions: A causal model agreeing with h; independence concerns causal parent relations among input variables, not merely statistical independence.
definitions.gloss: No input feature directly causes another input feature.
definitions.relation: Under agreement, collapses weak, strong and direct sufficiency; also collapses the paper’s dependence and causation variants.

definitions.quote: Elsewhere I have called this interpretation of sufficiency weak sufficiency (Beckers, 2021).
definitions.formula: \vec X=\vec x\text{ is weakly sufficient for }\vec Y=\vec y\iff\forall\vec u\in\mathcal R(\mathcal U):\ (M,\vec u)\models[\vec X\leftarrow\vec x]\vec Y=\vec y.
definitions.assumptions: Known deterministic strongly recursive causal model; no interventions on other variables; quantification over every context.
definitions.gloss: Setting the proposed cause guarantees the outcome across backgrounds while everything else follows its equations.
definitions.relation: Implied by strong sufficiency; equivalent to direct sufficiency under agreement and Independence.

definitions.quote: In the context of causal models I have coined this direct sufficiency (Beckers, 2021).
definitions.formula: \vec C=\mathcal V\setminus(\vec X\cup\vec Y);\qquad\forall\vec c\in\mathcal R(\vec C),\vec u\in\mathcal R(\mathcal U):\ (M,\vec u)\models[\vec X\leftarrow\vec x,\vec C\leftarrow\vec c]\vec Y=\vec y.
definitions.assumptions: Known deterministic strongly recursive causal model; arbitrary interventions on all remaining endogenous variables.
definitions.gloss: The proposed cause guarantees the outcome regardless of interventions on any other endogenous variables.
definitions.relation: Stronger than strong and weak sufficiency; strong sufficiency applies direct sufficiency to an entire protected network.

definitions.quote: I call the relevant notion of causal sufficiency at work strong sufficiency (Beckers, 2021), which can be formally defined as follows:
definitions.formula: \vec Y\subseteq\vec N\quad\land\quad\exists\vec n\supseteq\vec y:\ \vec X=\vec x\text{ is directly sufficient for }\vec N=\vec n.
definitions.assumptions: Known deterministic strongly recursive causal model; the network N is safeguarded from intervention and its whole assignment is determined by X=x.
definitions.gloss: The cause fixes a complete causal network containing the outcome, despite interventions outside that network.
definitions.relation: Intermediate between direct and weak sufficiency; forms the basis of sufficient explanations.

definitions.term: sufficient explanation; actual sufficient explanation; direct sufficient explanation; part of an explanation
definitions.quote: Using strong sufficiency we can define a sufficient explanation so that it specifies all the required elements for it to be action-guiding.
definitions.formula: \begin{aligned}(\vec X=\vec x,\vec N)\text{ is a sufficient explanation of }Y=y&\iff\vec X=\vec x\text{ is strongly sufficient for }Y=y\text{ along }\vec N.\\\text{It is actual in }(M,\vec u)&\iff(M,\vec u)\models\vec X=\vec x.\\\text{It is direct}&\iff\vec N=\{Y\}.\\\vec X'=\vec x'\text{ is a part}&\iff\vec X'\subseteq\vec X,\ \vec x'=\vec x|_{\vec X'}.\end{aligned}
definitions.assumptions: Known deterministic strongly recursive model; a selected safeguarded network. Actuality additionally requires a context.
definitions.gloss: An explanation states both a sufficient intervention and the network that must remain undisturbed; actuality and directness add explicit restrictions.
definitions.relation: Uses strong sufficiency; supplies the objects ordered by dominance and used in counterfactual explanations and actual causation.

definitions.quote: Of course we do not want to add redundant parts to a sufficient set, as a good explanation should be as concise as possible.
definitions.formula: E_i=(\vec X_i=\vec x_i,\vec N_i);\quad E_1\succeq E_2\iff\bigl(E_1,E_2\text{ explain the same }Y=y\bigr)\land\vec X_1\subseteq\vec X_2\land\vec N_1\subseteq\vec N_2;\quad E_1\succ E_2\iff E_1\succeq E_2\land\neg(E_2\succeq E_1).
definitions.assumptions: Two sufficient explanations in the same causal model. Definition 9 compares variable sets and does not separately require matching assigned values.
definitions.gloss: An explanation dominates another when it needs no more intervention variables or safeguarded variables.
definitions.relation: Defines the ordering used by good sufficient explanations and replacement.

definitions.quote: This allows us to define what makes for a good sufficient explanation of an observed output.
definitions.formula: \operatorname{Good}(E;M,\vec u,y)\iff E\text{ is an actual sufficient explanation of }Y=y\ \land\ \nexists E'\ne E:\ E'\text{ is an actual sufficient explanation of }Y=y\land E'\succeq E.
definitions.assumptions: Fixed causal setting and outcome, sufficient explanations and Definition 9 dominance. The definition says 'not dominated by any other', rather than 'not strictly dominated'.
definitions.gloss: A good actual explanation admits no other actual explanation requiring fewer or equal explanatory and safeguarded variables.
definitions.relation: Adds minimality to actual sufficient explanation; actual causes are particular parts of good sufficient explanations.

definitions.quote: Formally the causal notion that this third interpretation relies on is the latest definition of actual causation by Halpern, which is best understood as a generalization of counterfactual dependence in the following way.
definitions.formula: (M,\vec u)\models\vec X=\vec x\land\vec W=\vec w\land Y=y,\qquad(M,\vec u)\models[\vec X\leftarrow\vec x',\vec W\leftarrow\vec w]Y\ne y,\qquad\vec X\text{ minimal};\quad\vec W\text{ is a witness}.
definitions.assumptions: Known deterministic strongly recursive model and actual context; disjoint cause and witness variables; alternative values differ componentwise from actual values.
definitions.gloss: Changing a minimal cause changes the outcome when a specified witness retains its actual values.
definitions.relation: Generalizes standard and direct counterfactual dependence; corresponds to modified HP actual causation, but differs from the paper’s Definition 15.

definitions.quote: Here I will call this relation direct counterfactual dependence.
definitions.formula: \vec W=\mathcal V\setminus(\vec X\cup\{Y\})\quad\text{in Definition 11};\qquad(M,\vec u)\models[\vec X\leftarrow\vec x',\vec W\leftarrow\vec w]Y\ne y.
definitions.assumptions: Definition 11 actuality and minimality; all other endogenous variables can be held at their actual values.
definitions.gloss: Change the proposed cause while fixing every other endogenous variable except the outcome.
definitions.relation: Special case of generalized counterfactual dependence with the largest witness; connected to controlled direct effects.

definitions.quote: This relation is standardly referred to as counterfactual dependence (Pearl, 2009).
definitions.formula: \vec W=\varnothing\quad\text{in Definition 11};\qquad(M,\vec u)\models\vec X=\vec x\land Y=y,\quad(M,\vec u)\models[\vec X\leftarrow\vec x']Y\ne y,\quad\vec X\text{ minimal}.
definitions.assumptions: Known causal setting; no interventions beyond changing the proposed cause; other variables follow their equations.
definitions.gloss: Changing the cause changes the outcome without fixing any additional variables.
definitions.relation: Special case of generalized counterfactual dependence with an empty witness.

definitions.quote: Therefore I define counterfactual explanations as counterfactual analogs of sufficient explanations.
definitions.formula: \begin{aligned}\vec X=\vec x\text{ rather than }\vec X=\vec x'\text{ explains }Y=y\text{ relative to }(\vec W=\vec w,\vec N)\iff&\ ((\vec X=\vec x,\vec W=\vec w),\vec N)\text{ is an actual sufficient explanation of }Y=y\\&\land\exists y'\ne y:\ ((\vec X=\vec x',\vec W=\vec w),\vec N)\text{ is a sufficient explanation of }Y=y'.\end{aligned}
definitions.assumptions: Known causal setting; componentwise different alternatives; same witness values and safeguarded network in the factual and alternative explanations.
definitions.gloss: The actual intervention guarantees this outcome, while the alternative guarantees another outcome under the same safeguards.
definitions.relation: Combines two sufficient explanations; good counterfactual explanations characterize Definition 11 dependence existentially over witnesses and networks.

definitions.quote: Just as with sufficient explanations, we want an explanation to be as concise as possible.
definitions.formula: E_i=(\vec X_i=(\vec x_i,\vec x_i'),\vec W_i=\vec w_i,\vec N_i);\quad E_1\succeq E_2\iff\bigl(E_1,E_2\text{ explain the same }Y=y\bigr)\land\vec X_1\subseteq\vec X_2\land\vec W_1\subseteq\vec W_2\land\vec N_1\subseteq\vec N_2;\quad E_1\succ E_2\iff E_1\succeq E_2\land\neg(E_2\succeq E_1).
definitions.assumptions: Counterfactual explanations in one causal setting; comparison uses cause, witness and safeguarded-network sets.
definitions.gloss: Prefer explanations that require fewer changed variables, fixed witnesses and safeguarded variables.
definitions.relation: Extends sufficient-explanation dominance by adding a witness-set comparison.

definitions.quote: A counterfactual explanation is good if it is not dominated by any other counterfactual explanation.
definitions.formula: \operatorname{GoodCF}(E)\iff\operatorname{CFExplanation}(E)\land\nexists E'\ne E:\ \operatorname{CFExplanation}(E')\land E'\succeq E.
definitions.assumptions: Fixed causal setting, outcome and Definition 13 dominance; retains the paper’s non-strict 'dominated' wording.
definitions.gloss: No other counterfactual explanation uses fewer or equal cause, witness and safeguarded variables.
definitions.relation: Theorem 2 relates its existence to generalized counterfactual dependence.

definitions.quote: First I make precise how changing the values of some variables can turn a sufficient explanation into a better one.
definitions.formula: \begin{aligned}E&=((\vec X=\vec x,\vec W=\vec w),\vec N);\\\vec X=\vec x'\text{ can replace }\vec X=\vec x&\iff\exists E':\ E'\text{ sufficiently explains the same }Y=y,\ E'\succeq E,\ E'\text{ includes }(\vec X=\vec x',\vec W=\vec w).\end{aligned}
definitions.assumptions: A sufficient explanation, its partition into changed and retained assignments, and sufficient-explanation dominance. The replacement explanation need not be actual.
definitions.gloss: Alternative values can replace actual ones when they preserve the outcome in an explanation at least as economical.
definitions.relation: Non-replaceability distinguishes actual causes from arbitrary parts of good sufficient explanations.

definitions.quote: Therefore I define actual causes as parts of explanations that sit in between counterfactual and sufficient explanations: they are parts of good sufficient explanations such that there exist counterfactual values which would not have made the explanation better.
definitions.formula: \vec X=\vec x\text{ rather than }\vec X=\vec x'\text{ is an actual cause of }Y=y\iff\exists E:\ E\text{ is a good sufficient explanation of }Y=y\text{ in }(M,\vec u),\ \vec X=\vec x\text{ is part of }E,\ \neg\operatorname{Replace}_E(\vec x',\vec x).
definitions.assumptions: Known deterministic causal setting, good sufficient explanations, replacement criterion and componentwise distinct alternative values.
definitions.gloss: A cause belongs to a good sufficient explanation and has an alternative that cannot preserve that explanation’s guarantees.
definitions.relation: Weaker than counterfactual explanation; differs from generalized counterfactual dependence in Definition 11; largely equivalent to Beckers’s 2021 causation definition.

definitions.quote: An obvious strengthening of actual causation is to replace the existential quantifier over counterfactual values with a universal one, so that the actual values are the optimal values in terms of explanations.
definitions.formula: \exists E:\ E\text{ is a good sufficient explanation of }Y=y\text{ in }(M,\vec u),\ \vec X=\vec x\text{ is part of }E,\ \forall\vec x'\text{ differing componentwise from }\vec x:\ \neg\operatorname{Replace}_E(\vec x',\vec x).
definitions.assumptions: Known causal setting; one good sufficient explanation must resist every admissible alternative assignment.
definitions.gloss: The actual values cannot be replaced by any alternative in the relevant good explanation.
definitions.relation: Strengthens actual causation by universally quantifying over alternatives.

definitions.quote: Finally, replacing strong sufficiency with direct sufficiency offers a notion of direct causation .
definitions.formula: \vec X=\vec x\text{ is a direct cause of }Y=y\text{ in }(M,\vec u)\iff\vec X=\vec x\text{ is part of an actual direct good sufficient explanation of }Y=y.
definitions.assumptions: Known causal setting; goodness and actuality; a direct sufficient explanation has safeguarded network containing only the outcome.
definitions.gloss: A direct cause belongs to a minimal actual explanation that does not rely on an intermediate safeguarded network.
definitions.relation: Proposition 3 gives an alternative making every direct cause an actual cause; direct causation need not imply optimal causation.

definitions.quote: Here as well do we find a growing influence of causal models, most prominently in the work on counterfactual fairness, which in its basic form can be characterized as the condition that an output should not standardly counterfactually depend – see Def. 11 – on a protected variable (Kusner et al., 2017; Loftus et al., 2018).
definitions.formula: \nexists\vec u,a,a',y:\ Y=y\text{ standardly counterfactually depends on }A=a\text{ rather than }A=a'\text{ in }(M,\vec u).
definitions.assumptions: Deterministic causal model, protected variable and standard counterfactual dependence. This is the paper’s characterization of prior fairness work.
definitions.gloss: Changing a protected attribute alone must never change the outcome.
definitions.relation: The paper replaces this dependence criterion with actual causation along unfair networks.

definitions.term: fair for A relative to PaM
definitions.quote: Concretely, I propose the following deterministic definition of fairness, which can easily be extended into a probabilistic definition by moving to probabilistic causal models.
definitions.formula: \nexists\vec u,y,a,a',\vec W,\vec w,\vec N:\ \operatorname{ActualCause}_{(\vec W=\vec w,\vec N)}(A=a\text{ rather than }A=a',Y=y;M,\vec u)\land\operatorname{Pa}_{\vec N}\subseteq\operatorname{Pa}_M.
definitions.assumptions: Known causal model, protected variable A, specified unfair-path set Pa_M and Definition 15 actual causation relative to witnesses and networks.
definitions.gloss: A protected attribute must never actually cause the outcome through a network consisting entirely of unfair paths.
definitions.relation: Alternative to path-specific counterfactual fairness; detects the paper’s example where counterfactual dependence misses discrimination.

---
key: beckers2025large
title: "Large Language Models as Nondeterministic Causal Models"
authors: "Beckers"
year: 2025
venue: "KR 2026 (accepted)"
url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.22297v2
checked: 2026-11-01
tags: [source:formal-sweep-2026-11-01, contribution:theory, motivation:explainability, motivation:auditing]
---
**TL;DR** Models language models as nondeterministic causal systems, making prompt counterfactuals accessible through ordinary sampling and expressing stability as an optional bias.
**Problem** Existing counterfactual generation depends on a particular sampling implementation and imposes additional constraints.
**Method** Nondeterministic causal semantics; autoregressive hierarchy-collapse proof; selection functions for biased counterfactuals.
**Findings** Changed-prompt counterfactual distributions equal observational distributions under the intended interpretation; stability can be imposed without Gumbel-specific constraints.
**Limits** Depends on the chosen stochastic semantics. Large output spaces complicate estimation; application-specific filters remain unimplemented. No empirical evaluation.

**Relations**

definitions.quote: For the present purposes we can get by with using a simplified definition of nondeterministic causal models, I refer the reader to (Beckers, 2025b,a) for the general definition and more discussion.
definitions.formula: M=(\mathbf V,G,P_M),\qquad P_M(\mathbf V)=\prod_{X\in\mathbf V}P_M(X\mid\mathbf{Pa}_X),\qquad G\text{ acyclic}.
definitions.assumptions: Specified variable domains and DAG; probabilities represent nondeterministic mechanisms rather than ignorance about deterministic mechanisms.
definitions.gloss: A directed acyclic causal system specifies stochastic mechanisms directly.
definitions.relation: Alternative to the deterministic causal-model representation; supports Definition 2 counterfactual semantics.

definitions.quote: This formalizes the simple idea that the only information the actual world gives us about counterfactual worlds is that the actual parents resulted in their actual children, and nothing more.
definitions.formula: \begin{aligned}P^{(x,\mathbf{pa}_X)}(X=x\mid\mathbf{pa}_X)&=1,\\P^{(x,\mathbf{pa}_X)}(X\mid\mathbf{pa}_X^*)&=P(X\mid\mathbf{pa}_X^*)\quad(\mathbf{pa}_X^*\ne\mathbf{pa}_X),\\P^{\mathbf v}(\mathbf V)&=\prod_{X\in\mathbf V}P^{(x,\mathbf{pa}_X)}(X\mid\mathbf{Pa}_X),\\P^*(\mathbf V^*=\mathbf v^*\mid\mathbf V=\mathbf v,\mathbf R^*=\mathbf r^*)&=P^{\mathbf v}(\mathbf V^*=\mathbf v^*\mid\mathbf R^*=\mathbf r^*).\end{aligned}
definitions.assumptions: Nondeterministic causal model, complete factual assignment and imposed counterfactual root values. Actual local input-output pairs are retained; unobserved parent settings retain prior mechanisms.
definitions.gloss: Preserve observed responses to actual parent values, but reuse the original stochastic mechanism for changed parent values.
definitions.relation: General nondeterministic semantics; reduces to simple semantics for the paper’s LLM representation and is recovered by unrestricted selection.

definitions.quote: In other words, the simple semantics states that the counterfactual distribution does not depend on the factual result at all and takes on the same form as the prior, factual, distribution.
definitions.formula: \forall\mathbf r^*,\mathbf v\text{ with }\mathbf r^*\not\subseteq\mathbf v:\quad P_M^*(\mathbf V^*=\mathbf v^*\mid\mathbf V=\mathbf v,\mathbf R^*=\mathbf r^*)=P_M(\mathbf V=\mathbf v^*\mid\mathbf R=\mathbf r^*).\qquad P^*(Y^*=y^*\mid Y=y,X=x,X^*=x^*)=P(Y=y^*\mid X=x^*)\ (x^*\ne x).
definitions.assumptions: Genuinely changed root input. Theorem 2 establishes the condition for the idealized autoregressive LLM representation, not arbitrary stochastic systems.
definitions.gloss: A changed-prompt counterfactual is distributed like an ordinary new run on that prompt.
definitions.relation: Special property of the general nondeterministic semantics; differs from conditioning on factual evidence in deterministic latent-noise models.

definitions.quote: Definition 4. A deterministic causal model M is a 5-tuple (V, U, G, f, PU ), where V and G are as before, U is a set of variables called exogenous (V are called endogenous), f is a function f : (u, r) → v mapping values for the exogenous and root variables to values of the endogenous variables such that r ⊆ f (u, r) (i.e., f is the identity function for R), and PU is a probability distribution over U satisfying positivity.
definitions.formula: M=(\mathbf V,\mathbf U,G,f,P_{\mathbf U}),\quad f:(\mathbf u,\mathbf r)\mapsto\mathbf v,\quad\mathbf r\subseteq f(\mathbf u,\mathbf r),\quad P_{\mathbf U}(\mathbf u)>0;\qquad\mathbf v=f(\mathbf u,\mathbf r)\text{ defines a solution}.
definitions.assumptions: Specified acyclic graph, deterministic response function, exogenous variables and positive exogenous distribution.
definitions.gloss: Outputs are deterministic once root inputs and latent background variables are fixed.
definitions.relation: Contrasts with nondeterministic causal models; implementations using pseudorandom generators admit this literal representation.

definitions.quote: Probabilities of counterfactuals – of the same restricted form as before – are now defined as:
definitions.formula: P^*(\mathbf v^*\mid\mathbf v,\mathbf r^*)=\sum_{\{\mathbf u:\mathbf v^*=f(\mathbf u,\mathbf r^*)\}}P(\mathbf u\mid\mathbf v)=\frac{\sum_{\{\mathbf u:\mathbf v^*=f(\mathbf u,\mathbf r^*),\ \mathbf v=f(\mathbf u,\mathbf r)\}}P_{\mathbf U}(\mathbf u)}{\sum_{\{\mathbf u:\mathbf v=f(\mathbf u,\mathbf r)\}}P_{\mathbf U}(\mathbf u)},\quad\mathbf r\subseteq\mathbf v.
definitions.assumptions: Deterministic causal model, specified latent-variable distribution and factual evidence of positive probability; the same latent values are used counterfactually.
definitions.gloss: Infer latent backgrounds from the observed run, then change the root input while retaining those backgrounds.
definitions.relation: Pearl-style semantics appropriate to deterministic mechanisms; generally not identified by an LLM’s observational distribution alone.

definitions.quote: Definition 5. Given a family of distributions P (Y|X), observed values x, y, and a counterfactual value x∗ , we define the set of stable values as
definitions.formula: \operatorname{St}(y,x,x^*)=\{y\}\cup\left\{y':\frac{P(y\mid x^*)}{P(y\mid x)}<\frac{P(y'\mid x^*)}{P(y'\mid x)}\right\}.
definitions.assumptions: Factual input-output pair, counterfactual input and conditional output probabilities. Ratios need defined denominators or a zero-probability convention.
definitions.gloss: Keep the factual output and alternatives whose relative probability increase exceeds its increase.
definitions.relation: Defines the allowed support for Counterfactual Stability and the stable selection function.

definitions.quote: Informally, CS means that all counterfactual values whose relative increase in prior probability – when moving from the actual to the counterfactual setting – is lower than that of the actual value are excluded.
definitions.formula: P^*(Y\notin\operatorname{St}(y,x,x^*)\mid y,x,x^*)=0.
definitions.assumptions: Conditional observational distributions, a factual input-output pair and the stable-value set. The formal strict inequality also excludes nonfactual ties.
definitions.gloss: The counterfactual distribution puts no probability outside the stable-value set.
definitions.relation: Optional restriction on counterfactual distributions; Gumbel-Max models impose additional constraints beyond stability.

definitions.quote: Definition 6. Given a causal model M and a variable X ∈ V, a selection function SX for X is a function that maps values (x, paX , paX ∗ ) to subsets of X’s domain that include x, and such that S(x, paX , paX ) = {x}. We define S := ∪{X∈V} {SX }, and call S a selection function for M .
definitions.formula: S_X(x,\mathbf{pa}_X,\mathbf{pa}_X^*)\subseteq\mathcal R(X),\quad x\in S_X(x,\mathbf{pa}_X,\mathbf{pa}_X^*),\quad S_X(x,\mathbf{pa}_X,\mathbf{pa}_X)=\{x\};\qquad S=\bigcup_{X\in\mathbf V}\{S_X\}.
definitions.assumptions: Known variable domains, factual local assignments and counterfactual parent assignments.
definitions.gloss: A selection function specifies which alternative child values are admissible after changing its parents.
definitions.relation: Parameterizes biased counterfactual probabilities, including unrestricted and counterfactually stable semantics.

definitions.quote: A selection function can be used to straightforwardly refine the general nondeterministic semantics from Definition 2: one simply conditions on the fact that counterfactual values are restricted to those in S.
definitions.formula: \begin{aligned}P_S^{(x,\mathbf{pa}_X)}(X\mid\mathbf{pa}_X^*)&:=P(X\mid\mathbf{pa}_X^*,X\in S_X(x,\mathbf{pa}_X,\mathbf{pa}_X^*)),\\P_S^{\mathbf v}(\mathbf V)&=\prod_{X\in\mathbf V}P_S^{(x,\mathbf{pa}_X)}(X\mid\mathbf{Pa}_X),\\P_S^*(\mathbf V^*=\mathbf v^*\mid\mathbf V=\mathbf v,\mathbf R^*=\mathbf r^*)&=P_S^{\mathbf v}(\mathbf V^*=\mathbf v^*\mid\mathbf R^*=\mathbf r^*).\end{aligned}
definitions.assumptions: Nondeterministic model, complete factual assignment and selection function; selected conditional events must have positive probability.
definitions.gloss: Restrict each counterfactual mechanism to selected outputs, renormalize, and combine the resulting local distributions.
definitions.relation: Generalizes Definition 2 through selection; described as Bayesianized Imaging.

definitions.term: unbiased nondeterministic semantics; counterfactually stable semantics
definitions.quote: Choosing S U defines the unbiased nondeterministic semantics, and choosing St defines the counterfactually stable semantics.
definitions.formula: S_X^U(x,\mathbf{pa},\mathbf{pa}^*)=\begin{cases}\{x\},&\mathbf{pa}^*=\mathbf{pa},\\\mathcal R(X),&\mathbf{pa}^*\ne\mathbf{pa};\end{cases}\qquad S_X^{\mathrm{St}}=\operatorname{St};\qquad P^*_{S^U}\text{ is unbiased},\quad P^*_{\mathrm{St}}\text{ is counterfactually stable}.
definitions.assumptions: Definition 7 construction; unrestricted selection is set-maximal subject to Definition 6. Stable selection uses local conditional distributions.
definitions.gloss: One specialization permits every alternative; the other limits alternatives to stable values.
definitions.relation: Unbiased semantics recovers Definition 2 and simple semantics for LLMs; stable semantics need not equal a Gumbel-Max counterfactual distribution.

definitions.quote: To see why, note first that all semantics under consideration satisfy consistency, meaning that PS∗ (Y ∗ = y|X = x, Y = y, X ∗ = x) = 1.
definitions.formula: P_S^*(Y^*=y\mid X=x,Y=y,X^*=x)=1.
definitions.assumptions: Factual input-output observation; counterfactual input equals the factual input.
definitions.gloss: Leaving the input unchanged reproduces the factual output with certainty.
definitions.relation: Shared by the compared semantics; explains why Definition 3 restricts simple semantics to genuinely changed inputs.

definitions.term: selection function for good counterfactual explanations
definitions.quote: For example, one natural method for generating good counterfactual explanations (Wachter, Mittelstadt, and Russell, 2017; Beckers, 2022) is to consider only those outcomes that are significantly different from the actual outcome – relative to the difference in the prompt – and yet are at least as likely under their respective prompt, resulting in the following selection function (where distance function d(., .) and threshold ϵ > 1 are task-specific parameters):
definitions.formula: S^{\mathrm{CE}}_{d,\epsilon}(y,x,x^*)=\left\{y':\frac{d(y',y)}{d(x^*,x)}\ge\epsilon\ \land\ P(y\mid x)\le P(y'\mid x^*)\right\},\qquad\epsilon>1.
definitions.assumptions: Task-specific distances, threshold, output probabilities and nonzero prompt distance. As printed, this proposed filter can exclude factual y and therefore need not satisfy Definition 6’s inclusion requirement.
definitions.gloss: Seek large output changes from small prompt changes without lowering the probability of the selected output.
definitions.relation: Proposed alternative to closeness-seeking counterfactual stability; implementation is deferred to future work.

**TL;DR** Uses counterfactual sufficiency and necessity to prune reasoning traces, producing demonstrations and training data that improve efficiency while generally preserving accuracy.
**Problem** CoTs omit essential steps or include costly redundant reasoning.
**Method** Correct-answer sufficiency gate; corrupted-step rollouts and validator-based PNS estimates; filtered demonstrations and supervised fine-tuning.
**Findings** Shorter traces generally retain or improve accuracy across mathematical and commonsense benchmarks; experts judge 84% of 50 sampled traces sufficient and necessary.
**Limits** Single-run correctness does not establish assumed perfect sufficiency. Results depend on validators, replacement quality, thresholds and rollout costs; difficult tasks and prompts remain sensitive.

**Relations**
- (none)

definitions.quote: Definition 1 (Chain-of-Thought (CoT) Reasoning [61]) Given an input Q = q, the Chain-ofThought (CoT) reasoning process generates the final answer A = a by sequentially deriving intermediate reasoning steps S = {s1 , s2 , . . . , sn }.
definitions.formula: P(A=a\mid Q=q)\propto\int P(a\mid s_1,\ldots,s_n,q)\prod_{i=1}^{n}P(s_i\mid s_{<i},q)\,dS.
definitions.assumptions: An autoregressive reasoning generator and answer generator; marginalization over possible reasoning traces.
definitions.gloss: An answer is generated through a sequence of intermediate steps, with answer probability marginalized over possible traces.
definitions.relation: Defines the reasoning objects whose sufficiency, necessity and PNS are subsequently evaluated.

definitions.quote: Definition 2 (Sufficiency, PS) Sufficiency measures whether the reasoning chain S = (s1 , . . . , sn ) is sufficient to produce the correct answer y.
definitions.formula: \operatorname{PS}(S,q)=P\bigl(A_{\operatorname{do}(S)}=y\mid A\ne y,\bar S,q\bigr).
definitions.assumptions: Known correct answer y, baseline chain bar S yielding an incorrect answer with positive probability, and meaningful counterfactual chain interventions.
definitions.gloss: Among baseline failures, how often would inserting this chain have produced the correct answer?
definitions.relation: Adapts Pearl’s probability of sufficiency to whole reasoning chains; distinct from the binary correctness proxy used by the algorithm.

definitions.quote: Definition 3 (Necessity, PN) Necessity quantifies whether a specific reasoning step st is required for producing the correct answer a = y.
definitions.formula: \operatorname{PN}(S,s_t,q)=P\left(A_{\operatorname{do}(s_{<t},\bar s_t,s'_{>t})}\ne y\mid A=y,S,q\right).
definitions.assumptions: A factually correct chain, specified incorrect replacement bar s_t and downstream continuation generated conditional on that replacement.
definitions.gloss: Given a successful chain, how often would corrupting this step and regenerating its continuation cause failure?
definitions.relation: Adapts probability of necessity to individual reasoning steps; under perfect sufficiency it supplies the paper’s PNS computation.

definitions.term: Probability of Necessary and Sufficient Cause (PNS) in CoT
definitions.quote: Inspired by the counterfactual definition [46], we define the Probability of Necessary and Sufficient Cause (PNS) for the step st as:
definitions.formula: S'=(s_{<t},\bar s_t,s'_{>t}),\qquad\operatorname{PNS}(S,s_t,q):=P(A_S=y,A_{S'}\ne y).
definitions.assumptions: Joint potential outcomes for original and replacement chains, a correct-answer target and a specified downstream-adaptive intervention. Bar s_t disambiguates the replacement step.
definitions.gloss: The original chain succeeds and the chain with the replaced step fails in the same counterfactual comparison.
definitions.relation: Joint necessity-and-sufficiency object. Appendix A identifies it by interventional differences under monotonicity, or by replacement failure probability under perfect original-chain success.

definitions.quote: We approximate CoT trace sufficiency as binary: PS = 1 if chain S yields the correct answer (equivalent to P (A = y | do(S), q) = 1; Appendix A), else PS = 0.
definitions.formula: \widehat{\operatorname{PS}}(S,q)=\mathbf 1\{\widehat y_{\mathrm{init}}=y\},\qquad\widehat y_{\mathrm{init}}=\operatorname{Rollout}(S,q).
definitions.assumptions: Ground-truth answer and a generated answer under the chain. One observed success does not itself establish success probability one.
definitions.gloss: Treat a chain as sufficient when its evaluated answer is correct.
definitions.relation: Operational proxy for PS; the paper invokes Appendix A’s perfect-intervention criterion to motivate the approximation.

definitions.quote: Each S is assessed by validation model V for coherence and logical integrity (beyond just final answer correctness).
definitions.formula: \widehat{\operatorname{PNS}}(S,s_t,q)=1-\frac1k\sum_{i=1}^{k}V\bigl(\bar S^{(i)}\bigr),\qquad\bar S^{(i)}=(s_{<t},\bar s_t,s_{>t}^{\prime(i)}).
definitions.assumptions: Original chain deemed sufficient; k replacement rollouts; replacements and descendants semantically disjoint from the originals; validator scores intended to represent successful coherent reasoning.
definitions.gloss: Estimate a step’s contribution as one minus average validity of alternative continuations.
definitions.relation: Estimates PNS using the perfect-sufficiency reduction; validator judgments go beyond the final-answer event in Definition 4.

definitions.quote: Nodes with PNS score below threshold α (and their downstream nodes) are pruned iteratively until all retained nodes satisfy necessity.
definitions.formula: s_t\text{ retained}\iff\widehat{\operatorname{PNS}}(S,s_t,q)>\alpha;\qquad s_t\text{ skipped otherwise}.
definitions.assumptions: A chain passing the sufficiency gate, an estimated PNS score and chosen threshold alpha. Algorithm 1 skips ties.
definitions.gloss: Keep a step only when its estimated causal contribution exceeds the chosen threshold.
definitions.relation: Turns the PNS estimator into the pruning rule; thresholded empirical necessity differs from a universal logical necessity claim.

definitions.quote: Definition 5 (CoT Exogeneity) When generating each reasoning step st , the generation of the current step depends only on the previous reasoning steps s<t and the question q, and not on any external variables.
definitions.formula: P(s_t\mid\operatorname{do}(s_{<t}),q)=P(s_t\mid s_{<t},q).
definitions.assumptions: The previous reasoning and question capture the relevant causes of current-step generation; interventions are interpreted as specified by the paper.
definitions.gloss: Conditioning on a reasoning prefix gives the same step distribution as intervening to impose it.
definitions.relation: Used in the paper’s PNS identification arguments and claimed perfect-intervention/full-sufficiency equivalence.

definitions.quote: This condition states that altering a reasoning step to an incorrect version cannot result in correcting a previously incorrect final answer. Equivalently, whenever the modified chain S yields a correct answer, the original unaltered chain S must also yield a correct answer, ensuring monotonic progression toward correctness.
definitions.formula: \forall t,\bar s_t:\quad P(A_S\ne y,A_{\bar S}=y)=0,\qquad\bar S=(s_{<t},\bar s_t,s'_{>t}).
definitions.assumptions: Joint potential outcomes under original and corrupted-step chains; applies to every considered step and corruption with regenerated downstream reasoning.
definitions.gloss: Corrupting a step can never repair an answer that the original chain would get wrong.
definitions.relation: Together with exogeneity, yields the PNS difference formula in Lemma 2; Lemma 3 instead assumes perfect original-chain success.

definitions.quote: This means the intervention do(S) guarantees A = y in all worlds compatible with q.
definitions.formula: \text{Perfect Intervention}:\ P(A=y\mid\operatorname{do}(S),q)=1;\qquad\text{Full Sufficiency}:\ \operatorname{PS}(S,q)=1.
definitions.assumptions: Appendix A.4 assumes exogeneity and positive baseline failure probability. Its converse argument additionally treats the correct chain as robustly successful; exogeneity alone does not generally establish the claimed equivalence.
definitions.gloss: Perfect intervention guarantees success everywhere; full sufficiency guarantees correction within the specified baseline-failure condition.
definitions.relation: The paper claims these criteria are equivalent and uses that claim to motivate its PS gate; they should remain distinct from single-run correctness.

definitions.term: ground-truth PNS; validator mean absolute error
definitions.quote: Specifically, we report the mean absolute error (MAE) between the estimated PNS values and ground-truth labels, where ground-truth PNS is defined as 1 for reasoning chains judged by experts to be both necessary and sufficient.
definitions.formula: \operatorname{MAE}=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left|\widehat{\operatorname{PNS}}_i-g_i\right|,\qquad g_i=1\text{ for chains experts judge both necessary and sufficient}.
definitions.assumptions: Expert-annotated samples and validator-based PNS estimates. The quoted definition specifies the positive label; coding of every other annotation is not explicitly detailed there.
definitions.where: Appendix J, Validator Accuracy and Robustness, [P681]
definitions.gloss: Compare estimated PNS with human reasoning-quality labels using average absolute error.
definitions.relation: A human-label validation proxy for the PNS estimator, rather than direct observation of Definition 4’s joint counterfactual probability.

**TL;DR** Defines natural direct, indirect and path-specific causal effects for nonlinear systems, and gives conditions for identifying natural effects from data.
**Problem** Variable fixing cannot isolate indirect effects or express important policies about causal pathways.
**Method** Structural counterfactuals; nested mediator interventions; path-specific equation modifications; identification proofs.
**Findings** Defines natural effects beyond linear models and derives experimental and observational identification conditions. Total effects generally require reverse-transition decompositions.
**Limits** Natural effects need additional causal assumptions; randomization alone generally does not identify them. General path-specific effects can remain unidentified even in Markovian models.

**Relations**
- (none)

definitions.quote: We will use the counterfactual notation Yx (u) to de­ note the value that Y would attain in unit (or situa­ tion) U = u under the control regime do(X = x). See Pearl (2000, Chapter 7) for formal semantics of these counterfactual utterances.
definitions.formula: Y_x(u):=\text{the value of }Y\text{ in unit }U=u\text{ under }\operatorname{do}(X=x).
definitions.assumptions: Structural causal model supporting interventions and unit-specific outcomes; background unit u remains fixed.
definitions.gloss: The outcome this particular unit would have under a specified intervention.
definitions.relation: Basic potential-outcome notation used in all controlled, natural and path-specific effects.

definitions.quote: The causal relationship that is easiest to interpret, define and estimate is the total effect.
definitions.formula: P(Y_x=y)=P(Y=y\mid\operatorname{do}(X=x));\qquad\operatorname{TE}(x,x^*;Y)=E(Y_x)-E(Y_{x^*}).
definitions.assumptions: A structural intervention semantics; reference level x* for contrasts; population distribution over units for expectations.
definitions.gloss: The overall outcome distribution under an intervention, or its mean change relative to a reference intervention.
definitions.relation: Combines direct and indirect pathways. In nonlinear models, Theorem 3 decomposes it using an effect for the reverse transition.

definitions.quote: A variable X is said to have a controlled direct effect on variable Y in model M and situation U if there exists a setting Z = z of the other variables in the model and two values of X, x"' and x, such that =
definitions.formula: \exists z,x^*,x:\quad Y_{x^*z}(u)\ne Y_{xz}(u).
definitions.assumptions: Known unit-level structural model; controllable setting z for other variables. Restricting Z to Y’s parents other than X leaves the definition unchanged.
definitions.gloss: Changing X can change this unit’s outcome even while the other relevant variables are fixed.
definitions.relation: Qualitative counterpart of the controlled direct-effect magnitude in Definition 2; differs from naturally choosing each unit’s mediator setting.

definitions.quote: Given a causal model M with causal graph G, the controlled direct effect of X on Y in unit U = u and setting Z = z is given by
definitions.formula: \operatorname{CDE}_z(x,x^*;Y,u)=Y_{xz}(u)-Y_{x^*z}(u).
definitions.assumptions: Structural model, fixed unit u, reference x*, specified mediator setting z and a numeric outcome scale. Z contains Y’s parents other than X.
definitions.gloss: The unit’s outcome difference between two X settings while mediators are fixed at z.
definitions.relation: Quantifies Definition 1. The paper also permits ratios or proportional differences as alternative magnitude conventions.

definitions.quote: (Average controlled direct effect) Given a probabilistic causal model (M, P(u)), the con­ trolled direct effect of event X = x on Y is defined as:
definitions.formula: \operatorname{CDE}_z(x,x^*;Y)=E(Y_{xz}-Y_{x^*z}).
definitions.assumptions: Probabilistic causal model and population distribution P(u); the same prescribed z is used across units. Identification requires appropriate experiments or causal assumptions.
definitions.gloss: Average the controlled direct-effect contrast across the population.
definitions.relation: Population counterpart of Definition 2; contrasts with average natural direct effect’s unit-specific mediator settings.

definitions.quote: (Unit-level natural direct effect; qualitative) An event X x is said to have a natural direct effect on variable Y in situation U if the following inequality holds
definitions.assumptions: Unit-level structural model supporting nested counterfactuals; reference x*; mediators fixed at the values that this same unit would attain under x*.
definitions.gloss: Changing X matters when mediators retain this unit’s own reference-condition values.
definitions.relation: Natural counterpart of qualitative controlled direct effect; variable-level effect exists when some pair x*, x satisfies the inequality.

definitions.quote: If one is interested in the magnitude of the natural direct effect, one can take the difference
definitions.formula: \operatorname{NDE}(x,x^*;Y,u)=Y_{x,Z_{x^*}(u)}(u)-Y_{x^*}(u).
definitions.assumptions: Numeric outcome, unit u and nested structural counterfactuals sharing the unit’s background conditions.
definitions.gloss: Measure the outcome change from changing X while preserving the unit’s reference mediator behavior.
definitions.relation: Quantifies Definition 4; its population expectation is Definition 5.

definitions.quote: (Average natural direct effect) The average natural direct effect of event X on a response variable Y, denoted N DE(x, x*; Y), is de­ fined as
definitions.formula: \operatorname{NDE}(x,x^*;Y)=E(Y_{x,Z_{x^*}})-E(Y_{x^*}).
definitions.assumptions: Probabilistic structural model, population distribution, reference x* and nested potential outcomes. Identification needs assumptions beyond ordinary treatment randomization.
definitions.gloss: Average the direct effect while each unit keeps its own mediator values under the reference intervention.
definitions.relation: Population version of Equation (5); differs from average controlled direct effect by natural rather than uniform mediator assignment.

definitions.quote: (Unit-level indirect effect; qualitative) An event X = x is said to have an indirect effect on variable Y in situation U = u if the following inequal­ ity holds
definitions.assumptions: Unit-level structural model and reference x*; X stays at x* while mediators receive their values under x.
definitions.gloss: The outcome changes when only the mediator response to changing X is transferred to the reference condition.
definitions.relation: Natural indirect counterpart of Definition 4; no analogous variable-fixing controlled indirect effect is supplied.

definitions.quote: Taking the difference between the two sides of Eq. (18), we can define the unit level indirect effect as
definitions.formula: \operatorname{NIE}(x,x^*;Y,u)=Y_{x^*,Z_x(u)}(u)-Y_{x^*}(u).
definitions.assumptions: Numeric outcome and nested unit-level counterfactuals; the mediator values under x are evaluated while X is fixed at x*.
definitions.gloss: Measure the outcome change caused by transferring the intervention-induced mediator values alone.
definitions.relation: Quantifies Definition 6 and averages to Definition 7.

definitions.quote: (Average indirect effect) The average indirect effect of event X = x. on variable Y, denoted NIE(x,x*; Y), is defined as
definitions.formula: \operatorname{NIE}(x,x^*;Y)=E(Y_{x^*,Z_x})-E(Y_{x^*}).
definitions.assumptions: Probabilistic structural model, population distribution and nested counterfactuals. Experimental or observational identification requires the conditions analyzed in Section 3.6.
definitions.gloss: Average the outcome change from altering mediator behavior while preserving the reference treatment.
definitions.relation: Population version of Equation (19); generally not TE minus same-direction NDE, although that additive relation holds in linear models.

definitions.quote: Let G be the the causal graph associated with model M, and let g be an edge-subgraph of G containing the paths selected for effect analysis. The g-specific effect of x on Y (relative to reference x*) is defined as the total effect of x on Y in a modified model M; formed as follows.
definitions.formula: \begin{aligned}PA_i&=\{PA_i(g),PA_i(\bar g)\},\\f_i^*(pa_i,u;g)&=f_i\bigl(pa_i(g),pa_i^*(\bar g),u\bigr),\qquad pa_i^*(\bar g)=PA_i(\bar g)_{x^*}(u),\\\operatorname{SE}_g(x,x^*;Y,u)_M&=\operatorname{TE}(x,x^*;Y,u)_{M_g^*}.\end{aligned}
definitions.assumptions: Structural model and graph, selected edge-subgraph g, fixed unit u and reference intervention x*. Inputs along excluded edges are replaced by their original-model reference values.
definitions.gloss: Allow influence through selected edges while supplying reference-world inputs along the excluded edges.
definitions.relation: Generalizes natural direct and indirect effects; unlike those special cases, some path-specific effects remain unidentified even in Markovian models.
